YOUR AUTOGENIC TRAINING
Choose a Module
SubCat01_Text:
Autogenic Training is a scientifically recognized relaxation method developed in the 1920s by the Berlin psychiatrist Johannes Heinrich Schultz. It is based on self-suggestion. By repeatedly mentally reciting certain formulas, like ("My arm is very heavy" or "My breathing is calm and even"), you can put your body and mind into a state of deep relaxation.

Effects on Body and Mind
Autogenic Training can reduce stress, relieve inner tension, and enhance concentration. When practiced regularly, it supports regeneration, improves sleep, and can alleviate psychosomatic complaints. On a mental level, it helps to organize thoughts, find inner calm, and enhance well-being.

Influence on the Autonomic Nervous System
The autonomic nervous system controls vital bodily functions such as heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, and digestion – largely without our conscious intervention. Autogenic Training has a regulating effect on this system by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, which is responsible for relaxation and recovery. At the same time, the excessive activity of the sympathetic nervous system – responsible for stress reactions such as rapid heartbeat or muscle tension – is reduced.

Examples of Control through Autogenic Training
  • Cardiovascular System: By using the formula 'My heart beats calmly and regularly', pulse rate can decrease, and blood pressure and heart rate stabilize.
  • Breathing: With 'My breathing flows calmly and evenly', breathing can be deepened and slowed, promoting inner calm.
  • Muscles: 'My arms and legs are pleasantly heavy' can relieve muscle tension and induce physical relaxation.
  • Temperature Regulation: 'My right arm is very warm' influences blood circulation and can warm cold hands or feet. Through this self-regulation, Autogenic Training becomes a powerful tool to positively influence physical and mental well-being.
AT_Basics_Instruction:
The basic exercises form the foundation for all advanced autogenic training techniques. They develop body awareness, inner calm, and reliable regulation of the nervous system. Only with a stable foundation can more complex practices be learned safely and sustainably.

Why the order matters: The exercises are designed so each step builds on the previous one. The set order first creates general relaxation, then breathing and heart exercises establish safe bodily centering, before visualization, heaviness, and warmth evoke deeper physical responses. The solar plexus work at the end stabilizes and integrates the experience. Following the order increases effectiveness and reduces the risk of overwhelm.

Goals and effects of each basic exercise:

  • 1. General relaxation: Establishes a relaxed, secure baseline. The aim is to release physical tension and turn attention inward.
  • 2. Breathing exercise: Calm, even breathing stabilizes the autonomic nervous system, improves oxygenation, and reduces acute stress reactions.
  • 3. Heart exercise: Perceiving and calming the heartbeat enhances self-regulation and the sense of safety in the body.
  • 4. Visualization exercise: Targeted inner imagery supports imagination, shifts emotional appraisal, and prepares for deeper suggestions.
  • 5. Heaviness exercise: Promotes muscular relaxation and grounding — the body feels heavy and secure, which reduces nervousness and inner restlessness.
  • 6. Warmth exercise: Experiencing inner warmth improves circulation, releases tension, and strengthens a sense of well-being.
  • 7. Solar plexus: Aims to activate a calm, centered energy in the body’s core; it integrates earlier effects and strengthens self-efficacy and stability.
Conclusion: The basic exercises are not optional extras — they are essential. A systematic practice in the recommended order creates the physical and mental groundwork that significantly enhances the success of advanced exercises. Consistency, calmness, and respecting personal limits are crucial.

Anxiety-Text:
Anxiety

is a natural response to stress or perceived danger, characterized by feelings of worry, nervousness, or fear. It can manifest in various forms, ranging from mild unease to severe panic attacks. While occasional anxiety is a normal part of life, chronic or excessive anxiety can interfere with daily activities and overall well-being.

General Social AnxietyIn generalized social anxiety disorder, also known as generalized social phobia, the fear extends to a variety of situations. Sufferers are not only anxious in a specific moment but feel uncomfortable in almost all social interactions. The central fears are:
  • Fear of negative evaluation: The feeling of being critically scrutinized, judged, or rejected by others.
  • Fear of embarrassment: The worry of appearing awkward in social situations, saying something wrong, or showing visible signs of anxiety, such as blushing, sweating, or trembling.
  • Fear of authority figures: The uncertainty in interacting with superiors, teachers, or other people in positions of power.
  • Fear of being the center of attention: The discomfort when drawing attention to oneself, whether by giving a speech, answering a question in a group, or even eating or drinking in public.
  • General everyday insecurity: Sufferers feel very insecure and tense in everyday social situations like making small talk with strangers or participating in group activities.
These fears often lead affected individuals to avoid social situations, which reinforces their isolation and further solidifies the anxiety.

Specific social anxieties focus on the fear of certain, narrowly defined social situations. Unlike generalized social anxiety, which affects a wide range of interactions, the fear here only arises when confronted with a particular situation. Those affected do not have problems in other social contexts that do not involve this specific challenge.

The most common specific anxieties are:
  • Public Speaking: Fear of giving presentations, speeches, or lectures in front of a group.
  • Eating or Drinking in Public: The fear of being watched and negatively judged by others while eating or drinking.
  • Writing or Signing in Front of Others: The worry that one's handwriting will tremble and be perceived as a sign of weakness.
  • Using Public Restrooms: The fear of being heard or judged while using a restroom.
  • Interacting with Authority Figures: The fear of interacting with superiors, teachers, or other people in positions of power.


Common symptoms of anxiety include:
  • Restlessness or feeling on edge
  • Rapid heartbeat
  • Excessive worrying
  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Muscle tension
  • Sleep disturbances
Anxiety disorders are the most common mental health disorders and can be triggered by a combination of genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. They often develop in response to stressful life events, trauma, or ongoing stressors.

Treatment for anxiety typically involves a combination of psychotherapy, medication, and lifestyle changes. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is particularly effective in helping individuals identify and change negative thought patterns that contribute to anxiety. Medications such as antidepressants or benzodiazepines may also be prescribed to manage symptoms. Additionally, practices like mindfulness meditation, regular exercise, and adequate sleep can help reduce anxiety levels.
GenAnxiety-Text:
Generalized Anxiety Disorder


Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a widespread mental illness characterized by persistent and excessive worries and anxieties. People with GAD often find it difficult to control their worries, which can lead to significant impairments in daily life. Typical symptoms include constant nervousness, muscle tension, sleep disturbances, and problems with concentration.

The causes of GAD are diverse and can include genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. Stressful life events, such as the loss of a loved one or professional challenges, can contribute to the development of GAD.

The treatment of Generalized Anxiety Disorder typically includes psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which aims to identify and change negative thought patterns. In some cases, medications such as antidepressants or anxiolytics may also be prescribed to alleviate the symptoms. With the right support and treatment, people with GAD can learn to manage their fears and lead a fulfilling life.

Autogenic Training can help with Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) by releasing deeply rooted physical and mental tension. The constant worry in GAD often leads to physiological symptoms like muscle tension, gastrointestinal issues, or insomnia. Through targeted autosuggestions such as “My body is completely heavy” or “My breath is calm and steady,” users learn to consciously soothe these physical reactions. This sends a relaxation signal to the nervous system and breaks the vicious cycle of anxiety and tension. On a cognitive level, autogenic training helps to stop the “thought carousel.” Users learn to shift their focus away from their worries and concentrate on the physical sensations of relaxation. This practice trains the mind to gain distance from thoughts and regain a sense of inner control. It is an active way to reduce excessive worry and sustainably improve quality of life.
SocialAnxiety-Text:
Social Anxiety Disorder

Social Anxiety Disorder is a widespread mental illness characterized by an intense fear of social situations. People with social anxiety disorder often fear being negatively evaluated or judged by others, which can lead to significant stress and avoidance of social interactions. This fear can affect various areas of life, including work, school, and personal relationships.

Generalized Social AnxietiesIn generalized social anxiety disorder, also known as generalized social phobia, the fear extends to a variety of situations. Sufferers are not only anxious in a specific moment but feel uncomfortable in almost all social interactions. The central fears are:
  • Fear of negative evaluation: The feeling of being critically scrutinized, judged, or rejected by others.
  • Fear of embarrassment: The worry of appearing awkward in social situations, saying something wrong, or showing visible signs of anxiety, such as blushing, sweating, or trembling.
  • Fear of authority figures: The uncertainty in interacting with superiors, teachers, or other people in positions of power.
  • Fear of being the center of attention: The discomfort when drawing attention to oneself, whether by giving a speech, answering a question in a group, or even eating or drinking in public.
  • General everyday insecurity: Sufferers feel very insecure and tense in everyday social situations like making small talk with strangers or participating in group activities.
These fears often lead affected individuals to avoid social situations, which reinforces their isolation and further solidifies the anxiety.

Specific Social Anxieties focus on the fear of certain, narrowly defined social situations. Unlike generalized social anxiety, which affects a wide range of interactions, the fear here only arises when confronted with a particular situation. Those affected do not have problems in other social contexts that do not involve this specific challenge. The most common specific anxieties are:
  • Public Speaking: Fear of giving presentations, speeches, or lectures in front of a group.
  • Eating or Drinking in Public: The fear of being watched and negatively judged by others while eating or drinking.
  • Writing or Signing in Front of Others: The worry that one's handwriting will tremble and be perceived as a sign of weakness.
  • Using Public Restrooms: The fear of being heard or judged while using a restroom.
  • Interacting with Authority Figures: The fear of interacting with superiors, teachers, or other people in positions of power.

Typical symptoms of social anxiety disorder include:
  • Intense fear of social situations
  • Avoidance of social interactions
  • Physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating, or nausea in social situations
  • Low self-esteem and excessive self-criticism
The causes of social anxiety disorder are diverse and can include genetic, environmental, and psychological factors. These fears often develop in childhood or adolescence and can be intensified by traumatic social experiences.

The treatment for social anxiety disorder usually includes psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which aims to identify and change negative thought patterns. In some cases, medications such as antidepressants may also be prescribed to alleviate the symptoms. With the right support and treatment, people with social anxiety disorder can learn to manage their fears and lead a fulfilling life.
Depression-Text:
Depression

Depression is a common and serious mental illness, marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest, and various emotional and physical symptoms. Everyday tasks can feel overwhelming, and many affected people struggle with feelings of hopelessness or worthlessness. Causes are diverse and may include genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors.

Typical symptoms of depression include:
  • Persistent sadness or emptiness
  • Loss of interest in activities once enjoyed
  • Changes in sleep or eating patterns
  • Exhaustion and lack of energy
  • Difficulty concentrating or making decisions
  • Feelings of guilt or worthlessness
  • Thoughts of death or suicide
Treatment often combines psychotherapy, medication, and self-help strategies. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) helps to identify and change negative thought patterns, while antidepressants can restore balance in the brain. With the right support, many people experience significant improvement and regain quality of life.

Common forms are the classic depressive episode, marked by low mood and lack of energy, and atypical depression, which can involve increased sleep and appetite. Autogenic Training (AT) can be supportive by bringing the body into deep relaxation. It helps calm the nervous system and regulate functions like sleep and heart rate. Through focused autosuggestions such as “My body is full of calm and strength,” negative thought patterns can be interrupted, restoring inner control and resilience. AT thus strengthens the mind-body connection and supports both mental and physical health.

depression_01_01-text: Depression is increasingly seen as a disease of civilization, fueled by constant demands, high workloads, and permanent availability. Daily life often feels burdensome and draining, reinforcing a cycle of hopelessness. The affirmation “I find lightness in my everyday life” helps redirect attention to moments that are less dominated by pressure. This shift in focus can interrupt dysfunctional thought patterns that intensify feelings of heaviness. By regularly anchoring the idea of lightness, individuals strengthen their ability to reframe situations and cultivate greater psychological flexibility. This flexibility is crucial for breaking depressive cycles and restoring a sense of relief in daily life.

depression_02_01-text: A central feature of depression is anhedonia—the loss of pleasure and motivation. Everyday activities are often experienced as meaningless and empty. The affirmation “I take small steps toward joy” counters this perception by emphasizing gradual progress instead of sudden, unrealistic change. Even minor positive actions activate reward-related brain circuits, reinforcing the sense of being capable. Over time, this incremental re-engagement can restore emotional responsiveness and reduce the pervasive sense of paralysis. In this way, small steps lay the groundwork for rebuilding stability and rediscovering satisfaction in life.

depression_03_01-text: Depression frequently leads to reduced drive and diminished energy, which reinforces self-critical thoughts. The feeling of being unable to act strengthens the perception of worthlessness. The affirmation “I regain motivation” targets this cycle by fostering the belief that inner activation is possible. It strengthens the expectation of being able to take initiative again. This promotes self-efficacy, a psychological construct often impaired in depression. By repeatedly reinforcing positive self-attributions, individuals create a basis for renewed competence and disrupt the stagnation that characterizes depressive episodes.

depression_04_01-text: Depression often causes a breakdown of daily routines: responsibilities feel overwhelming, while joy and interest decline. The affirmation “I redesign my everyday life” supports reorganization and fosters a sense of agency. By highlighting the ability to actively influence one’s schedule, it reduces feelings of helplessness. Small, deliberate actions can function as behavioral interventions that reconnect individuals to their lives. This process not only restores structure but also helps counteract the sense of meaninglessness frequently experienced in depression.

depression_05_01-text: Resilience describes the ability to withstand stress without breaking under its weight. In depression, this protective capacity is often diminished. The affirmation “I strengthen my inner resilience” reinforces the idea that challenges do not inevitably lead to collapse. Research shows that activating personal resources such as confidence and hope has a stabilizing effect on mental health. By reframing difficulties as manageable, individuals develop a more adaptive perspective. This, in turn, lowers relapse risk and contributes to long-term emotional stability.

depression_06_01-text: Depression is often described with metaphors of darkness and emptiness, reflecting feelings of hopelessness. The affirmation “I take steps out of darkness” shifts attention toward progress and forward movement. This language activates neural pathways associated with goal-setting and future planning. Visualizing small steps encourages breaking free from rumination and withdrawal. As a result, individuals can open up to the possibility of change and reestablish a sense of direction, counteracting the immobilizing effects of depression.

depression_07_01-text: Depressive states often disrupt body awareness, leading to irregular eating patterns such as appetite loss or compensatory overeating. The affirmation “I eat mindfully” directs attention back to bodily signals. By practicing mindful eating, individuals regulate the connection between body and mind and foster healthier self-perception. Scientific studies show that mindfulness practices reduce dysfunctional behaviors and improve emotional stability. Eating is reframed not as compulsion or neglect but as an act of care, providing nourishment and supporting overall well-being.

depression_08_01-text: Depression often creates a conflicted relationship with food, marked by guilt, indifference, or compulsive behavior. The affirmation “I build a healthy relationship with food” promotes a re-evaluation of this fundamental need. Food is reframed from being a problem to being part of self-care. This cognitive shift supports emotional regulation and prevents destructive patterns from worsening depressive symptoms. A healthier relationship with eating not only strengthens self-esteem but also contributes to stabilizing energy levels, which are essential for managing depression effectively.

depression_09_01-text: Depression frequently drains individuals of vitality, leading to fatigue and a sense of emptiness. The affirmation “I recharge my energy” emphasizes the possibility of renewal. It introduces a positive expectation that supports both psychological and physiological regeneration. By cultivating the belief that energy can be restored, individuals activate recovery processes and experience daily tasks as less overwhelming. This helps disrupt the cycle of exhaustion and withdrawal that perpetuates depressive states.

depression_10_01-text: Even simple tasks can feel overwhelming in depression, intensifying feelings of inadequacy. The affirmation “I find strength for everyday life” strengthens the perception of capability. By reinforcing inner resources, it reduces the sense of being powerless. This process restores self-efficacy, which is essential for coping with depression. As individuals reconnect with their ability to act, everyday challenges are no longer experienced solely as threats but also as manageable opportunities for progress.

depression_11_01-text: Depression often results in social withdrawal and emotional numbness, leaving individuals disconnected from feelings of closeness. The affirmation “I rediscover heartwarming” reactivates positive emotional memory and fosters openness to connection. Neuropsychological findings suggest that re-engaging with positive emotions can stimulate the release of bonding-related neurotransmitters such as oxytocin. This creates a counterbalance to emotional blunting and strengthens the experience of meaning, warmth, and belonging in social relationships.

depression_12_01-text: Restlessness and rumination are common in depression, fueling emotional instability and fatigue. The affirmation “I find inner calm” introduces a stabilizing focus. It encourages the expectation that serenity is attainable despite external pressures. This reduces stress-related hyperactivation and strengthens a sense of self-control. Inner calm is not only a subjective relief but also a key factor for emotional regulation and long-term stabilization of depressive symptoms.

Bonus-Inhalte

In this section you will find exclusive exercises, inspirations, and additional materials available only here. Check back regularly – new highlights and information are added from time to time.
bonus_01_02:
AT Basic Exercises Complete
Exercise for Falling Asleep
bonus_01_01-text: In this compact exercise, all basic exercises of Autogenic Training are integrated into a single, unified exercise. This approach allows users to efficiently complete the full relaxation sequence without performing each exercise separately. Within the exercise, visualization can be individually adapted or replaced, creating a flexible and personalized experience. Furthermore, the exercise can be extended after the relaxation phase with targeted affirmations tailored to various issues, such as stress management, emotional stability, or behavioral change. The combination of standardized basic exercises, flexible visualization, and customizable affirmations not only enhances the effectiveness of self-regulation but also supports the long-term integration of relaxation into daily life. Research indicates that the ability to modify and extend exercises individually increases motivation to maintain regular practice, thereby producing sustainable effects on psychophysiological stress parameters.
